statement:
Let
$$f(x)=\frac{\sin\left((n+\tfrac12)x\right)}{\sin\tfrac12 x} \quad \text{for } 0<x\le\pi.$$

(i) Using the formula $2\sin\tfrac12x\cos kx=\sin(k+\tfrac12)x-\sin(k-\tfrac12)x$ (which you may assume), or otherwise, show that
$$f(x)=1+2\sum_{k=1}^{n}\cos kx.$$

(ii) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\,dx$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\cos x\,dx$.
solution:
(i) The identity $2\sin\tfrac12x\cos kx=\sin(k+\tfrac12)x-\sin(k-\tfrac12)x$ gives
$$2\sin\tfrac12x\sum_{k=1}^n\cos kx=\sum_{k=1}^n\bigl(\sin(k+\tfrac12)x-\sin(k-\tfrac12)x\bigr)=\sin(n+\tfrac12)x-\sin\tfrac12x,$$
by telescoping. Therefore
$$2\sin\tfrac12x\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^n\cos kx\right)=2\sin\tfrac12x+2\left(\sin(n+\tfrac12)x-\sin\tfrac12x\right)=2\sin(n+\tfrac12)x.$$
Dividing by $2\sin\tfrac12x$,
$$f(x)=\frac{\sin(n+\tfrac12)x}{\sin\tfrac12x}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^n\cos kx.$$

(ii) Integrating term by term,
$$\int_0^\pi f(x)\,dx=\int_0^\pi\left(1+2\sum_{k=1}^n\cos kx\right)dx=\pi+2\sum_{k=1}^n\left[\frac{\sin kx}{k}\right]_0^\pi=\pi,$$
since $\sin k\pi=0$ for every integer $k$.

For the second integral,
$$\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos x\,dx=\int_0^\pi\cos x\,dx+2\sum_{k=1}^n\int_0^\pi\cos kx\cos x\,dx.$$
The first term is $0$. Using $\cos kx\cos x=\tfrac12\bigl(\cos(k+1)x+\cos(k-1)x\bigr)$:
- for $k=1$, $\int_0^\pi\cos x\cos x\,dx=\int_0^\pi\cos^2x\,dx=\tfrac\pi2$;
- for $k\ge2$, $\int_0^\pi\cos kx\cos x\,dx=\tfrac12\int_0^\pi(\cos(k+1)x+\cos(k-1)x)dx=0$.

Hence
$$\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos x\,dx=2\cdot\frac\pi2=\pi.$$
hints: Use the given identity and telescope the sum of cosines.
Integrate term by term; all sine terms vanish at the endpoints.
For the cos x integral, use the product-to-sum formula and note only k=1 survives.
